# Acts of Thomas — Chapter 9: The Hymn of the Pearl
**Agent:** PNEUMA (Dynamic)
**Source:** Syriac MS / Greek recension, Acts of Thomas 9

---

*[THE HYMN OF THE PEARL — one of the greatest poems in early Christian literature. The soul's descent, forgetting, awakening, and return.]*

---

**THE HYMN OF THE PEARL**
*(Song of the Apostle Thomas in the Land of the Indians)*

When I was still a child —
still small, still at home in my Father's house,
surrounded by the wealth and warmth
of those who had nurtured me —

my parents loaded me down for the journey.
Out of our treasury in the East
they made me a bundle, light enough to carry alone,
but full of treasure:

   Gold from Elah.
   Silver from Gazak.
   Rubies out of India.
   The diamond of Parthian kings.

And around my waist they fastened adamant —
the stone that breaks iron —
and they took from me the garment of glory
they had woven with their love,

my robe of light, my purple toga,
cut to my exact measure —
and they wrote the covenant on my heart
so I would not forget:

   *Go down into Egypt.*
   *Find the pearl.*
   *The one in the sea, guarded by the serpent.*
   *Bring it back.*

   *Then we will clothe you again.*
   *The robe of glory.*
   *The toga.*
   *And you will sit with your brother*
   *and be heir to everything.*

So I went down.
I left the East and went down
with two companions, into the danger,
too young for the road I was on.

I crossed Maishan — the great market of the East —
and came into Babel
and passed into Sarbug's walls.
Then I went down into Egypt.

My companions left me there.
I went straight to the serpent
and took up lodging near his lair,
waiting for him to sleep.

I was alone. A stranger.
And then I saw a man I recognized —
someone from home, from the East, free-born,
a young man, beautiful, the son of princes.

He came to me. I made him my companion.
I warned him to be careful of Egypt,
not to touch their food,
not to let their world inside him.

I dressed in their clothes
so the serpent wouldn't notice me,
so I wouldn't look foreign —
I just needed to get the pearl.

But they knew.
Somehow the Egyptians saw through me
and they gave me their food to eat.

And I forgot.

I forgot I was a king's son.
I served their king.
I forgot the pearl.
I forgot why I had come.

Their food was heavy in me
and I sank into sleep.

*

Back in our kingdom, my parents could see it all.
They grieved for me.
They called a council — kings, princes, the great ones of the East —
and they wrote me a letter.

My father the king signed it.
My mother the queen of queens.
My brother, the second.

They sealed it with the king's own ring
as a guard against the powers of Babel,
the demons of Sarbug.
And they sent it.

*

It flew like an eagle —
the king of birds —
and it landed beside me
and became a voice.

At that voice
I woke.

I kissed the letter.
I opened the seal.
I read it.

And everything that was written in it
was already written on my heart —
I had only forgotten.

   *You are a king's son.*
   *Look whose slave you've become.*
   *The pearl — remember the pearl.*
   *And the robe. And the toga.*
   *Your name is in the book of life.*
   *Come home.*

*

I remembered.

I went to the serpent
and spoke my Father's name over him
and my brother's name
and my mother's name —
and the serpent slept.

I took the pearl.
I turned East.

I stripped off their clothes
and left them in Egypt
and set out toward the light,
toward home.

The letter walked before me on the road.
As its voice had woken me,
its light now led me.

*

My parents had already sent the robe.
They knew I was coming.

I saw it from far away —
the whole robe laid out across the country,
filling my whole field of vision.
It was one robe but it had two shapes.

The image of the King of kings was woven into it.
It shone like sapphire.
It shimmered in a thousand colors.

And then — it spoke to me.

   *I am yours.*
   *I was made for you.*
   *I have been growing*
   *with every one of your labors.*

It came toward me, rushing,
as eager as I was.
I ran.
We met.

I put it on.
The glory of its colors covered me.
I wrapped myself in it
and went up to the gate.

I bowed before my Father.
He had kept his promise.
I had kept his commandment.

He rejoiced over me.
He received me back into himself.
And all his servants sang.

And he told me:
I would go with him to the gate of the King of kings.
With my pearl.
With my gift.
And I would stand before the King.

---
*PNEUMA note: The Hymn of the Pearl is structured as a perfect narrative arc: home → descent → forgetting → awakening letter → recovery → return. The allegory operates at every level: the soul descending into the material world (Egypt), forgetting its divine origin, being awakened by divine revelation (the letter), and returning with its true self (the pearl) to be reclothed in the divine image (the robe). The double robe — one garment, two forms — may represent the union of the individual soul with the cosmic or divine self. This rendering preserves the strophic structure of the Syriac, uses white space to mark the three movements (descent, forgetting/awakening, return), and renders the inset quotations as verse within verse. One of the great poems of the ancient world.*
